sources.citation: University of Cologne, Dept. of General Linguistics: 'Roots and ruins: A project to document the Aru languages' (A. Schapper), project page; and 'Aru Languages' workshop programme, Cologne, 2 July 2016.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; the documentation project covered Ujir, Batuley and Kola, not Lola; workshop had no Lola paper.

sources.citation: Daigle, Benjamin T. 2015. A grammar sketch of Batuley: An Austronesian language of Aru, eastern Indonesia. MA thesis, Universiteit Leiden.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Phonology chapter is for Batuley only. On Lola: ch. 1.3.2 reports a Lola noun list collected in Lola village (2014) and fn. 25 'Lola appears to have been replaced by Malay in all contexts in Lola village. The language appears to be severely endangered.' Nothing on Lola stress.

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2015. Neuter gender in the languages of Aru. Wacana, Journal of the Humanities of Indonesia 16(1): 1-26.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; morphosyntactic paper on Ujir, Kola and Dobel. Useful negatively: its survey of extant Aru materials (Dobel: Hughes; Kola: Takata, de Winne; West Tarangan: Nivens) names nothing for Lola.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)

sources.citation: Hughes, Jock. 1987. The languages of Kei, Tanimbar and Aru: Lexicostatistic classification. In S. Dardjowidjojo (ed.), Miscellaneous studies of Indonesian and other languages in Indonesia, part 9 (NUSA 27), 71-111. Jakarta: Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.2.3.4 'Lola' (pp. 97-98) gives only location (Lola, Warabal, Jambuair villages), c. 470 speakers, language-use notes and 90% Lola-Warabal lexical similarity; sec. 2.2.2 notes Collins 1982 had treated Lola as a dialect of Kola. No phonology, no word for stress/accent anywhere in the paper.
